mcqs.question: Why do production systems often prefer item-based collaborative filtering over user-based CF?
options: Item-item similarity is typically more stable over time than a user's neighborhood of similar users, which can shift session to session
Item-based CF doesn't require a user-item interaction matrix at all
Item-based CF automatically solves the cold-start problem for new items
User-based CF cannot be computed for catalogs larger than 10,000 items
mcqs.explanation: Item-based CF wins mainly on stability: item-item relationships (co-rating patterns) change slowly, whereas a user's nearest neighbors can shift with every new interaction. Both methods need the same interaction matrix, neither solves new-item cold start, and there's no such catalog-size cutoff.

mcqs.question: In matrix factorization, what does multiplying a user's row in P by an item's column in Qᵀ actually produce?
options: The exact original rating, since P and Q are computed by copying values directly from R
A predicted rating (or preference score) for a user-item pair, including ones that were empty in the original matrix R
A similarity score between two users only, never between a user and an item
The number of times the user has interacted with that item
mcqs.explanation: The dot product of a user vector and item vector reconstructs an approximation of R, including previously-empty cells — that reconstruction of the unseen cells is the whole point of the technique. P and Q are learned by minimizing error on observed entries, not copied, and the dot product isn't a raw interaction count.

mcqs.question: Why does matrix factorization tend to handle sparsity better than raw neighborhood-based collaborative filtering?
options: It requires every user pair to share at least one rated item before making a prediction
It compresses the matrix to fewer rows so most cells are no longer empty
Two users can be connected through shared latent structure even without ever rating a common item directly, unlike neighborhood methods that need direct overlap
It ignores sparse users entirely and only recommends to users with dense rating histories
mcqs.explanation: Matrix factorization routes similarity through the learned latent space, so users can be 'close' via a chain of shared structure without any direct co-rated item — this is exactly what raw neighborhood methods can't do, since they rely on direct overlap. It doesn't require overlap, doesn't shrink the matrix's actual sparsity, and doesn't exclude sparse users.
